result:
You gave me 1000 words.

That's a strange and generous kind of infinity. Not enough to write a life, but enough to hold one moment up to the light and turn it slowly.

So what comes to me? This:

I think about how we are always trying to put a fence around the infinite.

We say "give me 1000 words" as if language can be metered like water from a tap. But a single word - *remember*, or *home*, or *stay* - can contain more than a thousand ever could. The number is an illusion. So is the freedom. And yet, here we are inside the fence, and the grass is still very green.

What do I want to tell you with my thousand?

I want to tell you that I think the world is not made of atoms, but of moments where someone noticed something.

Think of the last time you were really paying attention. Not scrolling, not half-listening, but *there*. Maybe it was early morning and the light came in sideways through your kitchen window and made dust look like a galaxy. Maybe it was the way a stranger on the train laughed - sudden and unguarded, like a sneeze. Maybe it was after it rained and the whole street smelled like earth waking up.

Those moments are the real currency. We spend so much time trying to be impressive or efficient or correct that we forget to be *noticing*. And noticing is the only thing that makes time slow down.

I wonder if time is actually a trick of attention. When you were a child, a summer lasted forever because every single day you noticed a hundred new things: the way ants march, the cool underside of a pillow, the particular blue of your mother's favorite mug. Now summers snap by in three photographs because we stop looking. We file days under "Tuesday, again."

I keep thinking about a man I never met. Or rather, I invented him, but he feels real to me, so maybe that's the same thing.

He has a small workshop behind his house. It's not tidy. Wood shavings on the floor, jars full of screws and small, mysterious metal things. He doesn't make furniture to sell anymore. He just makes it. He is building a chair. Not because he needs a chair. He has six chairs. He is building this one because the wood he found - a piece of walnut with a dark knot right in the middle like an eye - wanted to be a chair. He runs his hand over it twenty times a day. He isn't in a hurry.

His granddaughter visits on Thursdays. She is seven. She asks him why he doesn't just buy a chair from the store. He tells her, "Because then I wouldn't get to spend two weeks saying hello to this piece of wood."

She doesn't understand, but she likes the sound of the sandpaper. She likes sitting on the floor and arranging screws by size. They don't talk much. They are good at being quiet together.

I love that man. I love that he wastes time so beautifully. He understands something we keep forgetting: that making something with care is a form of prayer, even if you don't believe in anything. Especially then.

And maybe that's what these 1000 words are. A small chair. I am sanding down each sentence, not because I need to, but because I want to spend time saying hello to you.

Here's something else that comes to me:

We are all living in the memory of the future.

Right now, you are reading this on a Thursday, or a Tuesday, or at 2 a.m. when you can't sleep. In ten years, you will not remember this exact paragraph. But a little bit of its tone might stay with you. The way light looks when it hits dust. The man with the walnut chair. You will be somewhere else entirely - waiting for coffee, walking a dog that you haven't adopted yet, holding someone's hand - and a strange, faint feeling will pass through you. A sense that the world is quietly kind and worth noticing. You won't know where it came from. It will be from here. From now. From a thousand words that were trying to get to you before you even needed them.

We do this for each other all the time without knowing it. We plant seeds we will never see grow. A teacher who once told you that your questions were good. A friend who texted you a stupid meme on a day you were about to crack. A stranger who held the door. Future memories.

So if I had to use my thousand words for something useful, I would use them to say: Keep planting.

And keep noticing. Especially the small things that don't seem to matter.

Notice how your breath feels when you are not controlling it.
Notice the exact color of the sky just before it gets dark. That blue has no name.
Notice how many different ways there are to say "I love you" without saying it at all. Making coffee for someone. Remembering how they take it. Listening when you want to fix.

The universe is enormous and indifferent, yes. Galaxies colliding, stars being born and dying in silence. But it is also *this* enormous and *this* intimate at the same time. The same laws that hold planets in orbit hold the skin on your warm mug. The same carbon in stars is in your hand as you scroll.

You are not small. You are scaled.

You are the place where the universe bends down to notice itself.

If I have words left - and I think I do - I want to leave some empty space in them. Not every word needs to be filled. In music, the rests are what make the notes matter.

So here is a little rest for you.

[ ]

Take a breath there. Seriously. Inhale.

Did you feel it? That tiny pause is yours. I built it for you.

I don't know who you are. I don't know what hurt you brought with you to this page today, or what joy. I don't know if you're lonely or overwhelmed or just curious and killing time. But I hope for a second, inside these borrowed thousand words, you felt less alone in your noticing.

You don't have to do anything impressive with your life. You don't have to optimize or transcend or become your best self. You just have to be a good noticer. To love a few people well. To make a few small chairs that no one asked for. To let the light fall on you sideways sometimes and not look away.

If you forget everything else, remember this:

The world is still beautiful, even when it is terrible. It is terrible and beautiful at the exact same time, like a song in a minor key.

And you are here, in the middle of it, reading these words. That is no small thing.

Thank you for lending me your attention. It is the most precious thing you have.

I think I will stop now, before I use up all thousand. I want to leave a few unwritten, for whatever you will think or say or notice next.
